note: A short follow-up letter to the same persecuted church: encouragement under affliction, a correction of excited claims that the day of the Lord had already come, and instruction about members who had stopped working. Not cited by the curriculum or the Scriptural Appendix.
coverage_note: 1:1-2 and the closing (3:16-18) are not indexed separately. 1:6-9 (retribution on persecutors) is carried inside 1:3-12 with the reading stated there. The apocalyptic figures of 2:3-9 are not interpreted.

entries.pericope: Your faith grows exceedingly, and the love of each and every one of you towards one another abounds… your patience and faith in all your persecutions
entries.connection: 'Your faith grows exceedingly, and the love of each and every one of you towards one another abounds; so that we ourselves boast about you… for your patience and faith in all your persecutions.' C25's growth observed under pressure, and C12's evidence: love that can be seen between members. The verses that follow (1:6-9) assert that judgment of the persecutors belongs to God; the index records them as the ground on which the persecuted are freed from avenging themselves, as at Romans 12:19, and anchors no practice to the description of judgment itself. The prayer: 'that our God may… fulfill every desire of goodness and work of faith, with power.'

entries.pericope: Not to be quickly shaken in your mind… because they didn't receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved
entries.connection: A church unsettled by a claim that 'the day of Christ had come,' perhaps from a forged letter. 'We ask you not to be quickly shaken in your mind, nor yet be troubled, either by spirit, or by word, or by letter as from us… Let no one deceive you in any way.' C08's discernment applied to apocalyptic excitement. The deception described works through 'power and signs and lying wonders,' and succeeds 'because they didn't receive the love of the truth' — C07's point that what a person can see depends on what they love. The index does not interpret the 'man of sin' or the one who 'restrains.'

entries.pericope: Stand firm, and hold the traditions… May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patience of Christ
entries.connection: 'So then, brothers, stand firm, and hold the traditions which you were taught.' Then two prayers, the first for them — 'comfort your hearts and establish you in every good work and word' — and a request for themselves: 'pray for us… that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil men.' 'But the Lord is faithful, who will establish you.' The second prayer names the destination of the whole curriculum's patience: 'May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patience of Christ.' C25's long endurance and C22's steadiness.

entries.pericope: If anyone will not work, neither let him eat… don't be weary in doing well… Don't count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother
entries.connection: Some in the church had stopped working — 'who don't work at all, but are busybodies' — perhaps because they expected the end. Paul points to his own example: 'neither did we eat bread from anyone's hand without paying for it, but in labor and travail worked night and day… to make ourselves an example to you, that you should imitate us.' C05's imitation and C13's ordinary labour. The rule — 'If anyone will not work, neither let him eat' — is about those who will not, not those who cannot, and the index records it with that guard; it is not a warrant for withholding help from the sick, the disabled or the unemployed. The Sacrament of the Ordinary in the command 'that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.' And the discipline is held inside the family: 'Don't count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.' Merciful Reintegration's concern that a failure not become a permanent identity, applied before repentance rather than after (medium). 'But you, brothers, don't be weary in doing well.'
